headings.title: Introduction and Structural Architecture
headings.content: Cancellous bone, also known as spongy or trabecular bone, forms the inner core of bones and provides structural support without excessive weight. Unlike solid bone, it consists of a porous, honeycomb-like network of branching bony plates and rods called **trabeculae**. These spaces within the network are filled with bone marrow. The architecture is not random; trabeculae align precisely along lines of mechanical stress to resist loads coming from various directions. This specialized design allows the skeleton to remain lightweight while maintaining remarkable compressive strength.

headings.title: Microscopic Anatomy of Trabeculae
headings.content: At the microscopic level, trabeculae are composed of parallel lamellae, but they lack the true cylindrical **osteons** or Haversian systems found in compact bone. Because trabeculae are very thin, nutrients can easily diffuse from the surrounding marrow spaces directly through canaliculi into the osteocytes, eliminating the need for a complex central canal system. This direct access to blood supply keeps the bone cells alive and metabolically active despite the absence of blood vessels running directly through the bony matrix.

headings.title: Cellular Components
headings.content:
- **Osteoblasts**: Bone-forming cells located on the surface of trabeculae that synthesize the new osteoid matrix.
- **Osteoclasts**: Multinucleated giant cells responsible for bone resorption, residing in small depressions called Howship's lacunae.
- **Osteocytes**: Mature bone cells trapped within the matrix that monitor mechanical stress and regulate bone maintenance.
- **Osteoprogenitor cells**: Stem cells found in the endosteum that divide and differentiate into active osteoblasts.

headings.title: Comparison with Compact Bone
headings.content:
| Feature | Cancellous Bone | Compact Bone |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Location** | Inner cavity of bones, epiphyses | Outer shell of bones, diaphysis |
| **Porosity** | High (porous, spongy) | Low (dense, solid) |
| **Unit of Structure** | Trabeculae | Osteons (Haversian systems) |
| **Vascular Supply** | Surrounded by marrow blood spaces | Supplied by central and perforating canals |

headings.title: Hematopoiesis and Bone Marrow Storage
headings.content: The large open spaces between the trabeculae of cancellous bone house red bone marrow in active sites such as the vertebrae, sternum, and proximal ends of the femur and humerus. Red marrow is the primary site of hematopoiesis, where stem cells continuously produce red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. In long bones of adults, much of this red marrow is eventually replaced by yellow marrow, which consists mostly of adipose tissue and serves as an energy reserve.

headings.title: Adaptation to Mechanical Stress
headings.content: Cancellous bone undergoes constant remodeling in response to physical forces. According to Wolff's law, bone adapts and remodels its architecture based on the mechanical stresses placed upon it. When physical activity increases, osteoblasts deposit new bone matrix along the lines of stress, thickening the trabeculae. Conversely, prolonged immobility or weightlessness removes these mechanical stimuli, prompting osteoclasts to resorb bone tissue, leading to a rapid loss of trabecular mass and strength.

headings.title: Clinical Implications and Osteoporosis
headings.content: Because cancellous bone has a much higher surface area than compact bone, it is metabolically much more active and reacts more quickly to hormonal changes and systemic diseases. This high turnover makes cancellous bone the primary site affected by conditions such as osteoporosis, where trabeculae become thin, fracture easily, and lose their interconnectivity. Common sites for these fragility fractures include the femoral neck, distal radius, and vertebral bodies, which contain high proportions of spongy bone.
